opportunities.gap: The worked-example markup (two adjacent tags: AboutProjects) is used throughout to justify the symptom that runaway blue 'swallows everything below' the nav. Under the HTML5 parsing spec, when the parser meets the SECOND start tag while the first is still open, it acts as if a end tag had been seen (invoking the adoption agency algorithm), implicitly closing the first anchor. So in THIS exact two-anchor block 'About' renders as its own closed link and the styling does NOT propagate to paragraphs below the nav. The strong 'swallows every paragraph below' effect specifically requires a single unclosed followed by NON-anchor content. A browser-savvy reader/instructor can disprove the stated symptom for the shown markup. Affected: 05.mdx Opening Case (line 20), Core Concept (line 28), Worked Example Step 1 (lines 44-51), Textbook Walkthrough (line 93); 05.practice.json artifact_signal stem/explanation (lines 11,19); 05.misconceptions.json browser_blamed pattern.
opportunities.proposed_change:
Recommend option (a): make the unclosed anchor the LAST/only link before body content so the following paragraphs really are swallowed, OR add a paragraph after the nav and remove the second link's correctness so the open reaches non-anchor content. Concretely: change the Step-1 block to a single unclosed nav link followed by a body element, e.g. '
About

Welcome to my portfolio.

' so the open anchor swallows the

. Then the 'everything below turns blue' prose is literally true. If two links are kept, soften the prose: note the parser auto-closes the first anchor at the second , so the visible bug there is the odd/duplicated link rendering, while the runaway-swallow effect occurs when an unclosed anchor is followed by non-anchor content. Keep the practice item (artifact_signal) accurate by mirroring whichever markup is chosen; the option text 'wraps everything until the next close tag' is actually fine because the second is what supplies that next implicit close.

sources.cite: W3C HTML5 Tree construction, 'in body' insertion mode, start tag 'a' rule (W3C WD)
sources.finding: Spec text: 'If the list of active formatting elements contains an element whose tag name is "a" between the end of the list and the last marker... then this is a parse error; act as if an end tag with the tag name "a" had been seen, then remove that element from the list of active formatting elements and the stack of open elements if the end tag didn't already remove it.' I.e., a second <a> start tag implicitly closes the still-open first anchor, so the runaway effect does not reach content past the second <a>.

opportunities.gap: Internal inconsistency: the Opening Case, step-reveal 'Live check' reveal, Decision Rule live check, and Stronger Artifact Standard quote all turn on project links '404 from the subpath because the paths are absolute' with the remedy being relative paths. But the Worked Example (Step 1 tree, Step 4) and Textbook Walkthrough use a USER site at mlopez.github.io served from root (/), where absolute root paths like /assets/style.css do NOT 404. The absolute-vs-relative 404 trap is specifically a PROJECT-site phenomenon (username.github.io/reponame/). As written, the decisive failure the studio teaches cannot occur for the example artifact, undercutting the section's central proof. Confirmed against GitHub Docs: project sites publish under https://<owner>.github.io/<repositoryname> (a subdirectory base path), so a leading-slash absolute path resolves against the domain root and misses the /reponame/ prefix; user sites publish at https://<owner>.github.io (root) where the same path is correct.

sources.cite: GitHub Docs — About GitHub Pages (user/org vs project sites)
sources.finding: User/organization sites publish at https://<owner>.github.io (root); project sites publish at https://<owner>.github.io/<repositoryname>, i.e., served from a /reponame/ subdirectory base path.

sources.cite: Pluralsight — Fixing Broken Relative Links on GitHub Pages
sources.finding: On a project site under /repo-name/, absolute paths beginning with '/' resolve against the domain root and miss the repository subdirectory, breaking CSS/JS/image links; removing the leading slash (relative paths) or setting a <base>/baseurl fixes it. GitHub Pages does no runtime URL rewriting.
